entities.name: Charles de Montmorency
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Charles I de Montmorency (d. 1381), a scion of one of France's most ancient and powerful noble houses, emerged as a significant military and political figure during the tumultuous mid-14th century, a period deeply scarred by the Hundred Years' War and the Black Death. As a Marshal of France from 1344 to 1347, he held a pivotal command role under King Philip VI and later served Kings John II and Charles V, embodying the martial traditions of the French aristocracy. His career spanned a critical juncture when the French monarchy struggled against English incursions and internal factionalism, positioning him at the heart of royal efforts to consolidate power and defend the realm.

Montmorency distinguished himself early through military service, notably participating in campaigns in Brittany and the sieges of cities like Calais. Although he resigned his Marshal's baton in 1347, he remained a trusted advisor and military leader, commanding various royal contingents. He was captured by the English in 1356, prior to the catastrophic Battle of Poitiers, a testament to the continuous skirmishes and shifting fortunes of the war. His release and subsequent service to Charles V, particularly during the reconquest phases led by Bertrand du Guesclin, underscore his enduring loyalty and experience in a period marked by shifting allegiances and constant warfare.

His legacy is primarily tied to the continued ascent of the Montmorency family, whose prestige he helped cement through his high offices and military service. While not a figure who single-handedly altered the course of the Hundred Years' War, his consistent presence in the royal council and on the battlefield exemplified the resilience and adaptive strategies of the French nobility in the face of unprecedented national crisis. He contributed to the administrative and military structures that would eventually allow France to reclaim much of its lost territory and lay the groundwork for a stronger Valois monarchy.
